## Open

### F-733 — A group's injected libraries are only its own folder's

> _2026-11-14 · realm/blong-blob · open_

An injected library function is private to its handler group: the loader builds a group's `lib` from
the `library()` files in that group's own folder, so `orchestrator/upload` never saw
`orchestrator/blob/blobCipher.ts` even though its `handlerGroup.ts` imported the _type_ and its
handlers destructured `lib: {blobEncrypt}`. The type made it compile and the run threw
`Lib property 'blobEncrypt' not found` when the group was assembled — which happened only when a
test finally called `blob.upload.*` through the port, so the handlers had been broken since they
were written and the unit tests hid it by stubbing `lib`. The fix is a one-line re-export
(`export {default} from '../blob/blobCipher.ts'`) in the group that needs it. What would have caught
it earlier: a framework group that calls each handler once, rather than unit tests that construct
the api themselves.

### F-737 — A suite that carries the store closes a dev-dependency cycle

> _2026-11-14 · realm/blong-blob · open_

Wiring `blob` into a suite makes the two packages dev-depend on each other: `blob`'s browser tap
suite imports `@feasibleone/blong-access/browser.ts` for login and authorization, so an access suite
that carries the store closes the cycle and Rush silently skips the link — the symptom is a
`TS2307 Cannot find module '@feasibleone/blong-blob/server.ts'` right after a successful
`rush update`, whose output does warn about decoupling but not about which project it skipped. The
way out is to keep the dependency one-directional: the store is carried by the realm that owns the
records (party, sport), not by the realm that owns the identity tables, and a suite that needs both
is the test realm's business rather than a realm's. Checking `node_modules/@feasibleone/` in the
package is faster than reading the update output.

### F-740 — A browser-called method with no gateway route is refused as an encryption fault

> _2026-11-14 · realm/blong-blob · open_

Five faults stood between the widget and a photograph on the avatar, and no server test could see
any of them. The upload calls (`blob.upload.prepare`, `blob.upload.write`, `blob.upload.commit`,
`blob.upload.discard`) and the record read (`blob.blob.get`) had no `gateway/<group>/<method>.ts`
declaration, so there was no route, and the refusal that came back named the encryption rather than
the missing route. A route is authorised by the method name it carries, so the raw `PUT` needed
`blob.upload.write` in the capability even after the RPC trio was granted. The gateway's `rawBody`
switch is the process's, not a realm's: a child realm's config keys are its own block, so writing it
in `blob/server.ts` merged and was never read — it belongs in each hosting root. `prepare` stored an
empty scope list when the caller asked for none, and an empty list matches no cookie at all, so the
uploader could not read back what it had just written. And the shell only merges a realm's
`portalConfigGet` when the handler's group name ends in `.model`, `.component`, `.portal` or
`.action`; a `browser/orchestrator/scope/` group exported the hook and was never asked, so no scope
cookie was ever minted. Two lessons: a browser path is proved by a Playwright run and nothing less,
and each layer that reports a fault speaks in its own vocabulary — read the sequence of statuses
(404, 415, 403) rather than the last message.

### F-747 — A dispatch that answers nothing reads as a TypeError

> _2026-11-15 · realm/blong-blob · open_

Build #685 failed in three packages on the same shape: a test read `.removed` off the answer to
`blob.temp.cleanup` and got `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'removed')`. The message
names neither the call nor the answer, so the first question — did the sweep answer nothing, or did
the dispatch answer nothing on its behalf? — cannot be asked of the evidence. The assertion is now
`(answer?.removed ?? -1) >= 3` with the answer's JSON in the message, in the blob realm's `temp`
group and in `blong-int-adapter`'s s3 cleanup, so the next occurrence reports what came back.

What the run itself could not settle: every one of the four failures passed locally — the blob realm
256/256, `blong-int-adapter` 171/171, and the sport spec that creates an area — with the same
intents and with `CI=true`. A single slow runner (31 minutes for the tests job) is the likelier
explanation than a defect in the sweep, and one of the two blob failures was even classified
`timeout-under-load`. That is a hypothesis, not a finding: nothing in the bundle says the dispatch
timed out.

## Resolved

### F-736 — A realm cannot default its own port's settings

> _2026-11-14 · realm/blong-blob · resolved_

A realm's own `config` block is typed by the `validation` it declares, and a port's `activation`
block is typed by the contract it extends — so a realm cannot give its own port a development
default. `blob` wanted a committed dev key for `crypto.key` and `cookie.secret`, the way
`core/blong-gogo/src/devKeys.ts` does for the gateway: writing them under the realm's `config.dev`
fails with "`blobDispatch` does not exist in type", and writing them in the port's `activation.dev`
fails with "`crypto` does not exist in type Partial<Config<{namespace, imports}>>". What would
settle it: a port that declares its own settings schema (a `validation` beside the orchestrator, or
a documented way to extend the dispatch schema), so the component that owns a setting is the one
that can default it.

Resolved by typing the port: `orchestrator<IBlobConfig>()` in `orchestrator/blobDispatch.ts` makes
the activation block carry the realm's own settings, so the port now declares its dev `crypto.key`
and `cookie.secret` itself (committed, not secrets, the `devKeys.ts` rule). The realm is 242/242 and
ci-lint clean with it.

### F-738 — A declared k8s volume never reaches the generated tree

> _2026-11-14 · realm/blong-blob · resolved_

A `k8sVolumes`/`k8sIngresses` block declared in a component's `activation.default` does not reach
the generated tree for the blob realm, while the same shape works in the skill's example and in
`realm/blong-chat`'s adapters. Evidence: the claim was declared first on `adapter/store.ts` and then
on `orchestrator/blobDispatch.ts`
(`k8sVolumes: {blobStorage: {size, mountPath: '/var/lib/blong/blob'}}`), and
`blong ./realm/blong-sport/index.ts k8s` regenerated the tree — services and rbac were rewritten,
the deployment file was untouched, and `grep -r blobStorage system/` found nothing. `registryView`
reads `registry.getPort(id)?.config` and picks the k8s keys from it, so either `described.ports` is
empty by the time the k8s intent plans (the run stops every adapter before writing, and the plan may
be taken after) or the adapter instance's `config` no longer holds the activation slice at that
point. What would settle it: log the port list and one port's config when the plan is generated, or
run the generator before the stop phase.

Not the planner at all: a suite child with no config block does not load (D-637), and the blob child
was named under dev/integration but not under k8s — so there were no blob ports, and no ports means
no k8s contribution. Sport's k8s block now names blob, and blong ./realm/blong-sport/index.ts k8s
emits volumes/blobStorage.yaml and the deployment's mount.
